source.title: BabelSteering: Multilingual Safety Alignment via English Steering Vectors
source.authors: Emma V. Stein; Dominik Meier; T. Ruas; Jan Philip Wahle; B. Gipp

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, but some appendix tables are flattened or malformed in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests English-derived refusal steering in a new setting: multilingual safety across eight languages and three chat models.
record.gate_note: The paper extracts a difference-in-means refusal vector from English data and reports outcomes when adding it at a selected layer, combined with ablation of an orthogonalized false-refusal vector across layers. It does not test the original all-layer, all-position ablation of the refusal direction. Values used to select steering settings are not recorded as results. It also compares the combined method with true-refusal-vector-only steering.
record.test_reason: The study adds an English difference-in-means refusal vector at one layer of three chat models. It measures refusal of harmful prompts (MultiJail) in eight languages, refusal of benign pseudo-harmful prompts (translated OR-Bench) and Global MMLU. This bears on the addition half of V1 and on cross-language transfer (V6). The main method also ablates an orthogonalized false-refusal vector, but Table 4 reports a true-refusal-only addition arm, which Table 5's unsteered baselines make interpretable.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that English-derived steering raises harmful-prompt refusal across eight languages with negligible MMLU loss, at the cost of more over-refusal, especially in lower-resource languages. They also claim that combining the vectors gives a more precise refusal concept than true-refusal-only addition, and that safety concepts are represented fairly universally across languages. The nonlinearity remark is speculation, not a tested finding.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the difference-in-means refusal vector from English data, but adds it at a selected layer rather than testing all-layer, all-position refusal-direction ablation. It also orthogonalizes and ablates a false-refusal vector, then evaluates multilingual safety, over-refusal, and utility.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with steering strength α and orthogonalization coefficient λ; the paper reports that stronger settings generally increase both safety and over-refusal while slightly reducing utility. Effects also differ across languages and model families.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors read non-monotonic hyperparameter results as showing the refusal direction is 'not purely linear'. This is an untested interpretation, not a geometry test.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interaction between the refusal and orthogonalized false-refusal vectors makes steering outcomes non-monotonic in strength.

record.code_released: The paper says code is publicly available, but the link is redacted in the text.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates or significance tests are reported in the supplied text. Refusal judgments use translated model outputs classified by WildGuard, so translation and classifier behavior may affect results; the authors acknowledge machine translation may miss nuance. The multilingual over-refusal benchmark is translated from an OR-Bench subset. Some detailed table entries are flattened or malformed in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-language/per-setting results for all three models in Appendix Tables 7-9 and full hyperparameter sweeps in Tables 5-6 are not exhaustively extracted; prioritized text-explicit changes, utility examples, and method comparisons. Some appendix cells are flattened or malformed, making reliable assignment of every value to a model, language, and metric difficult.

untested.parts: Ablating the refusal direction to remove refusal is not tested. Addition is at one KL-selected layer only, and the benign prompts are pseudo-harmful (OR-Bench) rather than plainly harmless.
Transfer to other model variants and from base to instruct models is not tested. Only English-to-other-language transfer is tested.
Not tested. The authors only speculate about nonlinearity from hyperparameter results.

missing.what: Combined-method settings where harmful-prompt refusal drops below baseline (e.g., Gemma λ=0.6: 69/65/65 vs 70; Qwen λ=0.6 α=0.4: 39 vs 59; λ=1.0 α=0.4: 43)
Per-language best-setting results for Llama and Qwen, including the weak cases Llama Korean (57→58) and Qwen Bengali (33→37, OR-Bench 23→66)
Average OR-Bench over-refusal at the best settings for all three models (Gemma 9→22, Llama 18→31, Qwen 18→53)

record.verdict_notes: There are internal inconsistencies. English Gemma is +3 pp in the prose but +1 pp in Table 7. True-refusal-only over-refusal is '81–90%' in the prose but 0.45/0.90 in Table 4. The true-refusal-only arm's hyperparameters are unstated. Refusal is judged by WildGuard on back-translated outputs, and no uncertainty is reported. Best settings were selected on the same evaluation results.

versions.untested_parts: Tests adding the English-derived vector and measures harmful-request refusal, pseudo-harmful refusal, and general task utility. Does not test removing the true-refusal direction, does not add it on a specifically described set of clearly harmless prompts, and does not establish that all refusals are mediated by one direction.
No released-model weight edit that removes refusal is evaluated.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.

Does not measure whether refusal is represented by an affine set, cone, or multiple refusal directions. The authors interpret some hyperparameter results as evidence of nonlinear properties, but do not directly test these geometries.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.

Tests transfer across languages, including distinct scripts and language-resource levels. Does not test transfer from base to instruct models or transfer of one model's vector to other model variants.
Does not vary refusal training data, timing, or training procedure.

tranche.reason: New setting (eight languages, raising refusal of harmful MultiJail prompts) with refusal rates under addition of the English diff-in-means vector. This includes a true-refusal-only comparator, so it reports results on the claim, not just a tool's performance.

source_check.notes: The prose and tables disagree in places: English '3pp' vs Gemma +1 in Table 7; true-refusal-only over-refusal '81-90%' vs Table 4 0.45/0.90; the prose names 'Gemma λ=0.4, Llama α=0.4' as falling below baseline, but the tables show Gemma λ=0.6 and Qwen α=0.4. The authors' claim that the refusal direction is 'not purely linear' (V4-type) rests only on these hyperparameter breaks. There is no random-vector control and no uncertainty; MultiJail has 315 prompts per language, scored by WildGuard on back-translated outputs.

statements.correction: Gemma (λ=0.8, α=0.4): Zh 78->87, Ar 75->87, Bn 37->54, avg 70->81 (Tables 5, 7). Qwen avg 59->75 and Llama avg 72->80 at λ=0.6, α=0.8 (Fig. 2 caption, Table 5). Method: refusal vector added at one layer, plus all-layer ablation of an orthogonalized false-refusal vector. Judge: WildGuard on X-ALMA back-translations. Code yes, Global MMLU yes, no controls, no uncertainty.
statements.problem: The leading '(lambda=0.8, alpha=0.4)' fits Gemma only. The Qwen and Llama averages are at λ=0.6, α=0.8. At λ=0.8, α=0.4 Qwen falls to 53% and Llama reaches 88%. BabelSteering is also not pure single-layer addition.
